record.paper_title: Syzygies of projective varieties of large degree: recent progress and open problems.
record.original_question: Let X be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension n, let A be an ample divisor on X, let P be an arbitrary divisor, let B be a fixed twisting divisor, and set L_d = dA + P. For a fixed weight q with 2 <= q <= n, does there exist a constant C3 depending on X, A, B, and P such that the Koszul cohomology group K_{p,q}(X,B;L_d) vanishes for every p <= C3 d^(q-1) once d is sufficiently large? In other words, is the lower bound in the asymptotic non-vanishing theorem sharp up to a constant in the sense that all lower-index weight-q syzygies eventually disappear?

evidence.quote: Returning to the situation of Theorem 1.8, it is natural to ask what happens for those values of p outside the range governed by the statement. We conjecture that the lower bound appearing in (1.1) is actually the best possible in the sense that one has vanishing of pth syzygies for smaller p.
Conjecture 1.10. (Asymptotic vanishing). Fix q ∈ [2,n ]. In the situation of Theorem 1.8, there is a constant C3 (depending on X, A,B and P ) such that Kp,q(X,B :Ld) = 0 for p ≤ C3 ·dq−1 when d ≫ 0.
We consider the Conjecture to be the main open problem concerning the rough asymptotics of the Kp,q.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension $n \ge 2$. Let $A$ be an ample divisor on $X$, let $B$ be a fixed (twisting) divisor, and let $P$ be an arbitrary divisor on $X$. For each positive integer $d$, set
$$L_d \;=\; dA + P,$$
which is very ample for $d \gg 0$. For a coherent sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ on $X$ and a line bundle $L$ on $X$, the Koszul cohomology groups $K_{p,q}(X,\mathcal{F};L)$ are defined as the cohomology in the middle of
$$\wedge^{p+1} H^0(X,L) \otimes H^0(X,\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{q-1}) \;\to\; \wedge^{p} H^0(X,L) \otimes H^0(X,\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{q}) \;\to\; \wedge^{p-1} H^0(X,L) \otimes H^0(X,\mathcal{F} \otimes L^{q+1}).$$
Write $K_{p,q}(X,B;L) := K_{p,q}(X,\mathcal{O}_X(B);L)$.

Fix an integer $q$ with $2 \le q \le n$. Prove or disprove: there exists a positive constant $C_3 = C_3(X,A,B,P)$ such that, for all sufficiently large $d$,
$$K_{p,q}(X,B;L_d) \;=\; 0 \qquad \text{for every integer } p \text{ with } 1 \le p \le C_3 \cdot d^{\,q-1}.$$
Equivalently, show that the lower bound on $p$ in the asymptotic non-vanishing range for weight-$q$ syzygies is sharp up to a multiplicative constant, in the sense that all weight-$q$ syzygies with sufficiently small index $p$ eventually vanish.
artifact.status_search_result: The Ein–Lazarsfeld asymptotic vanishing conjecture for higher-weight syzygies $K_{p,q}(X,B;L_d)$ was proved by Jinhyung Park in the paper "Asymptotic vanishing of syzygies of algebraic varieties" (arXiv:2110.12419, published in Communications of the AMS, 2022). The proof reduces, via earlier work of Raicu, to a case on products of projective spaces which is handled in Park's paper. Subsequent work (e.g., arXiv:2305.15802, 2023) refines the complementary asymptotic nonvanishing statement, completing the asymptotic picture.

status_evidence.title: Asymptotic vanishing of syzygies of algebraic varieties
status_evidence.snippet: Asymptotic vanishing of syzygies of algebraic varieties — proves the Ein–Lazarsfeld conjecture that K_{p,q}(X,B;L_d) vanish for p of order d^{q-1}.
status_evidence.claim: Park proves the Ein–Lazarsfeld asymptotic vanishing conjecture for higher-weight syzygies.

status_evidence.title: Asymptotic vanishing of syzygies of algebraic varieties (Comm. AMS)
status_evidence.snippet: Published version in Communications of the American Mathematical Society, 2022.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is established in a peer-reviewed AMS publication.

status_evidence.title: Asymptotic nonvanishing of syzygies of algebraic varieties
status_evidence.snippet: Refines Ein–Lazarsfeld's asymptotic nonvanishing theorem; combined with the vanishing result, determines the asymptotic shape of resolutions.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent work treats the conjecture as established and complements it.
